main.text: Second Class.
Birds.

The original creation of birds has been discussed in §. 13; the difference between clean and unclean birds in §. 23; the difference in the nature of the eggs of clean and unclean birds in §. 18. Let it be noted here that Holy Scripture enumerates twenty unclean birds in Leviticus (11, 13—19) and twenty-one in Deuteronomy (14, 12—18), but adds to four of them, namely to the אנפה (§. 200), the איה (§. 196), the עורב (§. 205) and the נץ (§. 191), the word למינו, "after its kind," so that 24 unclean kinds of birds are named in Leviticus and 25 in Deuteronomy; however, the דיה, which occurs only in Deuteronomy, is taken (Chulin 63b) as identical with איה, so [p. 160] that in both books only 20 unclean birds are specifically mentioned. Now since that addition, being phrased generally, names no particular species, the Talmud subsumes many birds under that addition, or it designates many birds as unclean because they lack the characteristics necessary for determining cleanness (§. 23).
Many other birds are determined to be doubtful with respect to cleanness or uncleanness (see §. 211—219).
Sometimes unclean birds hatch the eggs of clean birds, and also vice versa (Chulin 138b).
In the partridge the male also broods (ibid. and below §. 264).

Not all eggs are capable of being hatched. One distinguishes 1) ביעי דדכרא (Beza 7a), eggs from the treading of the cock, 2) ביעי דספנא מארעא (ibid.), wind-eggs, which the hen conceives by lying in warm sand; these eggs are also called ביעי מוזרות (Chulin 64b); only the first-mentioned eggs are capable of being hatched.

Laid eggs are called ביעי דפחיא (Beza 7b); the eggs found in a slaughtered bird: ביעי דשחוטה (ibid.). The seed of the male is located in the white of the egg, namely at the flat or blunt end, from which the formation of the embryo begins (Chulin 64b*). Sometimes there is a drop of blood in the egg which, if it is in the yolk, spoils the whole egg; if it is in the white, the remaining part of the egg is permitted to be eaten (ibid.). If eggs of clean and unclean birds are cooked together, the clean eggs may be eaten, since eggs cooked in their shells impart no taste to one another (ibid.).
The strength of the eggshell when the egg is stood on its tip was known early on; thus an egg was sometimes placed under the foot of a bedstead in order to keep it level (Beza 3b).

Besides the use of the egg mentioned at the end of the preceding article, birds offer other and greater benefits. First, that of eating their flesh, although this admittedly ranks below the eating [p. 161] of the flesh of cattle; for, e.g., after bloodletting chicken is less advisable than the flesh of cattle (Meile 20b). The town dwellers, being the wealthier, consumed the most poultry (Bechoroth 10a).

A feeble old man was given a pound (ליטרא) of poultry to eat daily (Jerusalem Talmud Peah C. 8, fol. 21a). The excrement of some birds served medicinal purposes (§. 255). Some birds, such as the birds of prey, are trained for fowling (§. 192). With some birds threshing was even done (§§. 242 and 246). Of some birds the wings (§. 194), of others the talons (§. 197), and of still others the eggs were used for implements; in the latter case the eggs were covered with a glaze (§. 240). Even blown-out eggshells were used as oil containers for the lamp (Sabbat 29b).

The use of writing quills, however, was not yet known in the Talmudic age. Even in the 12th century some rabbis had scruples about writing the Torah scrolls with a bird's feather. Cf. Löw (המפתח part 1, p. 349); cf. finally Raschi on Gittin 69a, s.v. תלתא מבחלי, and above p. 45, note.
Parrots.
This Indian bird is called by Jehuda ha-Lewi (Kusari [=Judah ha-Levi, Sefer ha-Kuzari] 3, 5) בבגיא, or כפאגי (so Muskato reads for the corrupt גובא); Arabic بَبَّاجَاء [babbājāʾ]*).

In the Talmud (Chulin 62b) parrots bear other names. There it says: The bird שבור אנדרפטא is permitted to be eaten, the bird פירוז אנדרפטא is forbidden to be eaten. Aruch reads both times: אנדרפטא; but the word is explained by no lexicographer. I consider it to be compounded of Ἀνδρο [Andro] and Φατος [Phatos], and it has the sense of human-speaking. With this one may compare Aristotle (Thierg. [=Aelian, On the Nature of Animals (De natura animalium; German title Thiergeschichte)] 8, 14, 6), who says: In general all birds with hooked claws are short-necked, broad-tongued and inclined to mimicry, for to these belongs also that Indian bird [p. 162] the parrot, which is called Ἀνθρωπόγλωττον [anthrōpoglōtton] (human-speaking).

Among parrots, however, there are tame ones, which live on cereals, and also bold and rapacious ones (Voigt [=F. S. Voigt, Lehrbuch der Zoologie (Stuttgart 1835–40); the text names it (p. 9: "Voigt, Lehrb. d. Zool.")] l. c. [=loco citato: in the work cited above] 2, p. 81), which also live on meat. It is possible, then, that in our Talmud passage the distinction is made between tame and wild parrots; פירוז means wild, unruly, שברא on the other hand, simple (see Aruch s.v. שברא*).
The Owl.

In Babylon the bird קקותא was permitted to be eaten; in Meraba, on the other hand, whoever ate it was punished with blows, and there the same bird was called תחוותא (Chulin 63a). Raschi explains: A bird that cries at night and is called צואיטה, Chouette.
The former word is probably related to Κιχκάβη [Kichkabē].
The Little Owl.

Alongside the קקותא mentioned in the preceding article, two other forbidden birds are also named (Chulin 63a), the קיאי [p. 163] and the קקואי. Landau translates, without any justification: cormorant and pelican; apart from the fact that the pelican most probably bore a different name (cf. §. 227), it is also very strange that these two day-birds should be grouped with the owl. Buxdorf [=Johannes Buxtorf, Lexicon Chaldaicum, Talmudicum et Rabbinicum (Basel 1640)] (Lex. p. 2107) more correctly takes the Talmudic names as designations of night birds, and perhaps the two kinds of owlet, the little owl and the pygmy owl, are meant here. קקואי, for which Aruch reads קיקאי, may, being related to Cheveche, be the larger owlet, and קואי, after dropping the reduplication, the smaller owlet*).
The Eared Owl.

The great eared owl is called ינשוף in Hebrew (Lev. [=Leviticus] 11, 17) and קפופא in Talmudic. Its eyes are directed forward, it screeches at night, and its face resembles that of the cat (Nidda 23a). On Berachoth 57b Raschi says: It has cheeks like a human being and is called צואיטא, Chouette, a name which, to be sure, is used for the short-eared owl.

Its appearance in a dream is an evil omen because of the ugliness of the bird and its partial resemblance to a human being (ibid.); yet Raschi's explanation of the word קפופא is highly uncertain. On Chulin 63a he translates it as Chouette, but also as Chauvesouri; on Berachoth ibid., quite correctly, solely as Chouette; whereas ibid. 58b, quite differently, as Vulture (bearded vulture, see §. 113).
The Middle Eared Owl.
Berachoth 57b states: The appearance of the bird קדיא (or קדיא) in a dream is an evil omen because of its ugliness.

The Targumim use the Talmudic word to translate the Hebrew כוס (Lev. 11, 17), where Raschi explains it as ייב"ן, and in our Talmudic passage as ייב"ץ, Hibou. The French word designates the middle eared owl (the horned owl, also called the lesser eagle-owl).
The Sparrowhawk.

נץ (Chulin 42a and 63a). Raschi explains it both here and on Lev. 11, 16 as אישפריויר, Épervier, sparrowhawk. However, one manuscript of Raschi's commentary on that biblical passage has אושטוור, Astur, goshawk; the Tosephot (Chulin 63a. s.v. נץ) also maintain that נץ cannot mean sparrowhawk; and if we further note that Bochart [=Samuel Bochart, Hierozoicon, sive de animalibus Sacrae Scripturae (Lewysohn used the Frankfurt a. M. 1675 edition)] (Hieroz. [=Samuel Bochart, Hierozoicon (Frankfurt a. M. 1675 edition)] P. 2. lib. 2. c. 14, col. 245) translates נץ as Accipiter, the LXX as Ἱέραξ [hierax], Winer (R. Wb. [=G. B. Winer, Biblisches Realwörterbuch] s.v.) as goshawk, and likewise Rosenmüller [=E. F. K. Rosenmüller, Handbuch der biblischen Alterthumskunde, vol. 4, part 2 (Leipzig 1831)] (Bibl. Alterth. [=E. F. K. Rosenmüller, Handbuch der biblischen Alterthumskunde (Leipzig 1823–31)] vol. 4, part 2, p. 304), then, since the Greek and Latin word designates the entire genus of small hard-winged birds of prey, namely those that have four bare toes, hooked talons and a curved beak, the so-called genus of the strikers, the word נץ too may be a more general name for goshawk, sparrowhawk and falcon, which would at the same time explain the variants in Raschi mentioned above. Only in one passage (Chulin 42a) does Raschi contrast the goshawk with the sparrowhawk, so that נץ means only sparrowhawk; this passage is treated in the following article.
The Goshawk.

Chulin 42a states: The נץ kills small fowl, the גם large fowl, which Raschi expands in explanation: The sparrowhawk kills sparrows and doves, whereas the גם, i.e. אוסטוייר (Italian Astore), goshawk, kills chickens and geese.

Aruch, however, reads נז for גם and explains it as owl, or falcon. Mussaphia refers to Jonathan [=Targum (Pseudo-)Jonathan], who translates עזניה in Lev. 11, 13 as בר גוא*); but עזניה is a kind of eagle, cf. §. 194.

The Selicha for the second of the 10 days of penitence (cited in the Tos. [=Tosafot] Chulin ibid. s.v. דריסה) likewise reads: מדרס נז ונץ; Jesaias Pick, however, reads in the latter passage: מדרס גם והגז and understands נז as the falcon and גם as the vulture, for which reason Fürstenthal, in his commentary on the Selichoth, reads וואטור (Vauture) for אוסטוייר in the above passage of Raschi; but the vulture has [p. 165] other designations in the Talmud, and the goshawk is rightly called גס (large) in contrast to the sparrowhawk, since it is twice the size of the latter. Cf. also Isserels on Jore Dea §. 57, 3 and on it Sifte Cohen lit. 16, who translates גס as falcon and goshawk.

Finally, it should be noted that Raschi's statements regarding the prey of the two birds are not quite correct, for the sparrowhawk kills only small birds such as finches and sparrows, whereas the goshawk for its part seizes doves and chickens; accordingly one would have to strike out in Raschi doves among the small fowl and geese among the large fowl. Cf., however, Midrasch Rabba (Schir ha-Schirim fol. 17, col. d).
The Noble Falcon.

Besides the name גם, by which some designate the falcon (see §. 191), this bird, which is also called gyrfalcon and hunting falcon, has yet other names. In Chulin 63a the בר חיריא (son of whiteness) is also included under למינהו (after its kind), the addition which the Bible has after נץ (§. 190). Who, asks the Talmud, is the בר חיריא? It is, comes the answer, the שורינקא (shrike). Here the noble falcon is meant. It is brown above with whitish spots, sometimes entirely white (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 270), hence that name בר חיריא. It is trained for hunting, the hunter sitting on horseback with the falcon beside him, which he releases at the sight of another bird (Sabbat 94a). Perhaps it is also called בואי, of which it is related that David once went out to catch the בואי (Sanhedrin 95a), see Aruch s.v. שכר; yet the word is explained by Raschi as a place name, by others as prey*).
The Eagle.
The eagle
נשר

is the king of birds (Chagigah 13b); its flight is swift and it does not tire easily (Aboth 5, 20), [p. 166] yet it fears the flycatcher (§. 259). Fabulous is the legend that it catches the young chamois, which are born on high mountains and could easily meet their death by falling down, and brings them back to their mother (B. batra [=Bava Batra] 16b*).

It is the unclean bird κατ' ἐξοχήν [kat' exochēn], for it is a bird of prey (דורס, see the various explanations of this concept §. 23), it has no crop, has a single-skinned stomach and has no אצבע יתירה (Chulin 61a). The author of the ספר הברית**) copies the Talmudic statement without further explanation (ibid. Bl. 70, p. 2), although the last part of the statement presents much difficulty. Most take the אצבע יתירה to be the hind toe, which, however, is lacking in none of the species of eagle known to us; they differ only in the number of front toes, thus the golden eagle (Aquila imperialis) has not three but four front toes, yet each of the 10 species of eagle living in Europe has a hind toe; the Tosaphot also remark that the common eagle, אייגלא, Aigle, has a hind toe (Tos. Chulin 63a. s.v. נץ); one may therefore probably agree with the explanation of Nissim, who understands by אצבע יתירה the elongation of the front middle toe, which probably need not be the case with some species of eagle. The later decisors (see Peri Megadim on Ture Sahab Jore Dea §. 82, lit. 3), however, decide neither for the one nor for the other explanation***).
The eagle strangles its prey, which it devours at once without waiting for its death (Tos. Chulin 61a. s.v. הדורס).
On the title "Eagle!" cf. §. 107; on its love for its young p. 172, note.
The Osprey.

עוניה (Chulin 62a), and עז (Kelim 17, 14). The wings, which reach to the tip of the tail (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 278), were used for implements (Kelim ibid.). It never stays in places inhabited by humans (בישוב) (Chulin ibid.). Landau translates עז as sea eagle, אוז on the other hand as black eagle (A. Valera); but since the Jerusalem Targum renders עוניה by עוז or אוז, the latter word cannot be the black eagle, since this belongs precisely to the smallest species of eagle, whereas the above-mentioned use of the eagle's wings suggests only a large species of eagle.
The Ossifrage.

פרס, which is mentioned alongside the osprey (§. 194) in Chulin 62a. It too does not stay in inhabited places; the ossifrage belongs to the eagle genus and is the white-tailed sea eagle (Haliaëtos ossifragus), see Voigt l. c. 2. p. 277. It received its name because of its unruliness and ferocity; it stays especially on the seashore and preys on large mammals and birds, such as foxes, bustards, geese etc.
On the eagle species Perknopterus see the Appendix s.v. ירודות.
The Vulture.

After a lengthy discussion the Talmud comes to the conclusion that ראה, דאה, איה and דיה signify one and the same bird, but explains only the word ראה (to see), which indicates the sharp sight of the bird: "It can," it says there, "be in Babylon and nevertheless spot a carcass in Eretz Yisrael."

The gloss considers this statement a metaphor, but concedes the extraordinarily sharp sight of the bird. Now although all birds of prey have a sharp gaze, one can nevertheless see from Rashi (B. mez. [=Bava Metzia] 24b) which bird in particular is meant. Here it is related how the bird דיי took a piece of meat from the market and let it fall down into a garden. On this Rashi: עוף שקורין אוולטור והוא לשון דיה "the [p. 168] bird which is called Vulture (vulture), synonymous with דיה."

The sharp eye of the vulture is well known. In the first passage the Talmud adds that in the Orient there are a hundred species of unclean birds, all of which belong to the vulture genus; even if the round number is perhaps not to be taken literally (§. 12), it is nevertheless certain that the vulture genus is very numerous, most of which are found in Africa and Asia. Voigt l. c. 2. p. 282; cf. article Stork (§. 204).
The Griffon Vulture.

This vulture, also called the Contor or Condor, is the largest species of vulture; its outspread wings are said to measure eighteen feet, and its legs are as thick as a man's wrist (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 283). This bird is not mentioned explicitly in the Talmud, but in Rashi (Chulin 25b). The Talmudic passage says that certain implements were made from the claws (צפרנים, §. 54) of a bird; on this Rashi says that this is the גריפין, Griffon, griffon vulture.
The Egyptian Vulture.

Chulin 63a it says: The bird רחם (Lev. 11, 18; in Deut. [=Deuteronomy] 14, 17 it reads רחמה) is the שרקרק, but it is called רחם (love) because when it appears love (rain) is granted to the world. The name שרקרק was given to the bird on account of its cry, which sounds Schirkrek.

We leave the many divergent explanations aside (see הכתב והקבלה by J. Meklenburg on Lev. 11, 18), since, as Rosenmüller (loc. cit. p. 317) has demonstrated, the Arabic homophonous رخم [rakham] designates the Egyptian vulture. It is not much larger than our crow, but has long wings; its cry is hissing at first and ends in an unpleasant screeching.
One would accordingly have to imagine that natural sound שרקרק in such a way that the first notes שרק "Tschirk" and the after-sound רק "Reck" are heard as a subsequent screech.
Probably this bird makes its cry heard chiefly at the onset of the hoped-for Nile flood.

It should, however, [p. 169] not go unmentioned that in Arabic the bee-eater (Merops Apiaster) is called شِرِقْراق [shiriqrāq] (Schirikrakon), and here one may indeed choose between the two Arabic names, which correspond to the two names רחם and שרקרק, but which the Talmud assigns to one and the same bird.
In Cuvier this bird (Egyptian vulture) is called Perknopterus, but it is by no means identical with the Περκνόπτερος [Perknopteros] of the ancients, which is dealt with in the Appendix s.v. ירודות.
The Crane.
Kiduschin 44a it is said: Resch Lakesch cried out like a כרוכיא, on which Rashi: It is the translation of עגור (Jerem. [=Jeremiah] 8, 7) and is called גרואה Grue.

But if one compares Rashi on that biblical passage, then either סוס must be emended to עגור in our Rashi passage on the Talmud, or in that Rashi passage on the Bible the order must be שפנונא וסנונית וכורכיא; in any case כרוכיא is the crane and not, as Landau (Aruch s.v. קליאם) would have it, the raven. Landau lets himself be misled by the similarity of sound with the Greek Κόραξ [Korax]*); but the word far rather deserves to be compared with the Arabic كُرْكِيْ [kurkī], by which Saadias renders עגור at Jerem. l. c., and which in that language denotes the crane.
The remarkable structure of this bird's windpipe enables it to produce a piercing, loud cry, to which our Talmud passage alludes. See Voigt l. c. 2. p. 355.
The Heron.

Chulin 63a it says: אנפה is a cruel, high-flying bird, the actual דיה רגזנית (cruel דיה, see article Stork), but it is called אנפה because it is angry with its companions (אנף, whence the noun אף, anger), i.e., it fights and bites with them and is fierce. [p. 170]

Rashi cites this Talmud passage on Lev. 11, 19*) and adds: וכדומה לי שקוראין אותו איירון "and as I believe, it is the bird that is called Héron". Indeed the heron has a fierce nature; it is wild and given to biting (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 359). Even when it is shot lame, it defends itself furiously against the dogs and aims the thrusts of its beak at their heads, which is why one never sets a dog loose on it (Beumer: Populäre Naturgesch. p. 197). It has the same stilt-legs as the stork, with which it has much resemblance in general, and so it is rightly mentioned in Scripture next to that bird.
The Night Heron.
Chulin 63a it says: The bird אריכי שקי וירוקי, which has long legs (i.e. stilt-legs) and is ירוק in colour, may not be eaten.

As is well known, ירוק can mean green, yellow and blue (see Ture Sahab on Jore Dea §. 38, 1, and Isserels ibid. §. 188, 1). The night heron (Ardea Nycticorax) unites all these colours in itself. Head, back and shoulders are black, steel-blue and with a greenish shimmer; in the old male the belly is sulphur-yellow. It has stilt-legs and is rightly forbidden, since among the heron family the heron (§. 200) is expressly forbidden by Scripture.
The Common Flamingo.

Chulin 63a it says: The bird שקיטנא with long and red legs is permitted to be eaten. As proof (וסמנך) serves the מורומא. On this Rashi: There are two kinds of the bird שקיטנא; the one that has long legs (stilt-legs) and is red in body may be eaten, for as proof serves the bird מורומא, which is similarly shaped and generally known as clean. Aruch explains this latter word itself as a Persian one, by which every red and at the same time long object is designated. We are to take שקיטנא and מורומא here as identical and merely as provincialisms;

[p. 171] both names denote the first kind of flamingo, Phoenicopterus ruber. It is purple-red with an elongated neck and legs. Stretched out, its length amounts to 6 feet. It was probably considered clean because, owing to the webbing on its feet, it was counted among the family of water birds rather than that of the stilt birds. On the second kind mentioned above see the following article.
The Lesser Flamingo.

Chulin 63a it is said that the common flamingo (שקיטנא, §. 202) is permitted to be eaten, whereas the גוצי וסומקי (short and red) is forbidden to be eaten; the lesser flamingo, Phoenicopterus minor, lives in southern Africa and is smaller than the former (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 368). That the different kinds of one and the same bird family differed in ritual respect need not cause surprise, since in this matter the different regions did not always follow the same usage, cf. §. 186 on the owl, §. 210 on the starling, and §. 219 on the moorhen. Yet a distinction was also made, without any reason being given more precisely, among the kinds themselves, as with the parrot (§. 185) and with our bird.
The Stork.

Chulin 63a it is said: The חסידה is the דיה לבנה (white Daja), but it is called חסידה (the pious one) because it lovingly shares its food with its companions.*). That חסידה is the stork cannot be doubted. Rashi translates the word (Lev. 11, 19) by צינניה, Cigogne. The only question is how the Talmud could call the stork דיה לבנה, "white vulture"? One should note, however, that דיה, or דיי (B. mez. 24b, cf. above §. 196) denotes only the black or the common vulture; the notion [p. 172] of the name lies in the root word ראה, to hover, to fly high, and so by a more specific qualifying addition that notion can also be transferred to other high-flying birds of prey. The stork, which on the whole is white and black only on the wing-feathers, can rightly be called דיה לבנה "the white high-flying bird", while the heron (§. 200) on account of its fierceness is called דיה רגזנית "the cruel high-hovering bird". The two names of the stork are thus not an identity of essence but a mere identity of name, in the sense: one can call the stork the white vulture, which itself, on account of its lofty flight, is called דיה κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν [kat᾽ exochēn]. —

The name דיה לבנה corresponds perfectly to דיה חיורתא, whose gall possesses healing power against the poison of the scorpion's sting (Ketuboth 50a). Here Rashi translates the name by וושטול, evidently corrupt for ולטור, as ריו on B. mez. 24b; but also substantially incorrect, since here only the stork can be meant.

Pliny (h. n. [=Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Naturalis historia)] 29, 5, 33) says of the stork: Contra venena omnia cicouiarum ventriculus valet. "Against all poison the stomach of storks helps"; Harduin on the passage says that the inner lining of the stomach is meant here; that healing power against poisons was thus known early.

Finally it may be noted that the love (חסר) attributed to the stork is also related by Aristotle (l. c. 9, 14, 1). He says: Well known is the tale about the storks, namely that the old ones are in turn fed by their young.
The Raven.
עורב (B. Kama [=Bava Kamma] 92b), fem. עורבתא (Sabbat 67b) and פושקנצא (B. batra 73b), for which Aruch has פשקנצא.
Because of its croaking (§. 38) it is also called: קורקור (Baba batra 23a); because of its colour: עורב אוכמא (Chulin 63a).

Ravens love one another (Pesachim 113b), but (according to an old but erroneous notion) are without affection toward their young*), as long as these have not yet grown black feathers (Ketuboth 49b). As is well known, the young remain naked over the whole body for quite a long time (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 156). According to the Tosephot (ibid.)

[p. 173] that lack of affection is, however, said to be the case only with the common raven (§. 206), but not with the magpie (§. 210). Now since this latter kind of raven loves and feeds its young, one would call out to a man who will not feed his children: "He is worse than a raven!" (ibid.), just as one now says of a hard-hearted man: "He has a raven's heart!"

Meanwhile Providence cares for the young ravens, in that maggots arise from their own filth, on which they feed (B. batra 8a); the maggots even crawl into the ravens' mouths by themselves (Erubin 22a, cf. §. 470).

The adult ones feed on arum (Sabbat 126b*), as well as on fruits of trees and of the ground (Chulin 134b); that ravens seek out and devour the crops is also reported by Pliny (h. n. 17, 5, 4). They are attracted by blood (by the smell?), even by human blood, as on the occasion of bloodletting (B. batra 23a).
Of a black-haired youth it was customary to say: His locks are like the plumage of the raven (Chagigah 14a).

It also mates with the starling, since the latter belongs to its kind (B. Kama 92b**). During mating a mass of saliva flows from the mouth of the male into that of the female, and this is said to bring about fertilization (Sanhedrin 108b***).
If, in overcast weather, one wishes to know exactly when evening twilight begins, one should, when in the field, observe the ravens, which seek their night's roost at this time (Sabbat 35b).

The rich used to raise it as a domestic bird (ibid. 126b), but because of its filth it was kept away from the Temple at Jerusalem, which was accomplished by means of a scarecrow (Menachoth 107a). According to Aruch it was a figure such as gardeners are accustomed to make; Rashi explains the word כליה, as that scarecrow was called, as pointed pillars that were fixed on the Temple roof; the (so-called) Rashi commentary on M. Katan [=Moed Katan] 9a explains it differently†).
The [p. 174] raven's croaking (§. 38) served superstition as an omen (Sabbat 67b). Cf. §. 249.
The Common Raven.

This splendidly black bird seems to be meant in the Talmud passages cited in the preceding article (Chulin 63a and Ketuboth 49b) by עורבא אוכמא "black raven"; perhaps the Tosephot (Chulin 62a s.v. מפני) also mean it when they call it קורביל, Corbeau. It has an אצבע יתירה, see on this §. 193, and a crop.
All the statements mentioned in the preceding article also apply to this one.
The Sea Raven.
The Hebrew שלך (Lev. 11, 17) is explained by the Talmud (Chulin 63a) as: השולה דגים מן הים "which draws the fish out of the sea"; Rashi adds: והוא עורב המים "it is the water raven".
Onkelos on the above biblical passage therefore translates שלך by שלינונא "fish-lifter".

This is the cormorant, which is called Corvus marinus (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 414). Pliny (h. n. 10, 48, 68) calls the bird Phalacorax, which Harduin, though apparently incorrectly, identifies with Corvo aquatico (§. 209). Voigt describes the bird thus: The bill narrow, straight, with a hook at the end. The bird is trained for fishing by placing a ring around its neck, so that it cannot swallow the fish it catches and must spit them out. It is common on the Baltic. However, the Talmud seems to mean another species of this bird, for this bird also lives in China, and is called Louwa there, see Iselin's Historische Lexicon part 1 s.v. Cining. The bird is described there: It has a very long neck and a hooked bill like an eagle, it is as large as a goose and looks not unlike a raven. The training and the use of that ring are carried out there in the same way.
A Species of Raven.

Chulin 64a states that there is a species of raven whose eggs are similar to those of the dove, for which reason one may buy such eggs, which are pointed at one end and blunt at the other, only when one is certain that they are dove eggs.

From this, however, the species of bird can hardly be determined, for the eggs of all species of raven known to us already differ from dove eggs by their colour; they are mostly blue-green, brown-spotted, or olive-brown, whereas dove eggs are white. The 8 plates of egg illustrations by Oken give no information on the point in question, and only a complete collection of eggs might perhaps make its determination possible.
The Sea Crow.

קאת, which name is explained by קיק (Chulin 63a). Of it it is said (Sabbat 21a): We asked all seafarers, and they told us that in the coastal towns there is a bird called קיק. In Arabic the word of the same sound قِيق [qīq] means: crow, and Pliny calls the sea raven, or sea crow, Corvum aquaticum.

Compare with this the author of the מתנות כהונה (on Midr. [=Midrash] Esther fol. 119, col d); he says: I found in an old work the words: קברין שקנן על שפת הים. “A קברין, which nests on the shores of the sea.” Sachs (Beiträge zur Sprach- und Alterthumsforschung, 1st issue, p. 146) correctly conjectures that קברין is transposed for קרבין (Κόρβος [korbos], Corvus); but in the 2nd issue, p. 90, note 90, he retracts this opinion and takes קברין to be the “grave bird”, i.e. the night owl. But it is precisely this latter bird that lives and breeds in deciduous woods, and how should it be found nesting on the seashore? I take קברין to be a Phoenician word, transposed in the same way as Καβρώνοι [kabrōnoi] for קרבנין “sacrifices”; cf. my “Opfernamen” in the L. Bl. d. Orients [=Literaturblatt des Orients (Leipzig 1840–51), the literary supplement of Der Orient] 1849, col. 307. Cf. also §. 355, where a number of transposed words are given.*)
On קיק cf. further the Greek
[p. 176] קיק, which designates a certain sea bird, sea hen, seagull; see Or Ester s.v. קיק. —
The Magpie.

To the raven family belongs the עורב העמקי (Chulin 63a), a name which the Tosephot (Ketuboth 49b. s.v. הא) identify with עורב חיורי (white raven). This can only be the magpie, whose body, shoulders and vent are white. It loves the vicinity of human dwellings and has in itself a gentler character, which is why it is said of it that it loves its young (ibid.). Landau, less definitely, translates the name as white hooded crow.
The Starling.

זרזיר (Chulin 62a), Rashi: אשטורנול, Etourneau, Latin Sturnus. It belongs to the raven family (ibid.) and is therefore unclean; yet there was a place whose inhabitants used to eat the starling, to which they felt entitled because the starling has one of the distinguishing marks of a clean bird, namely a crop (ibid.). It mates with the raven and gave rise to the proverb: “Like associates with like” (ibid. 65a). It is striking that the starling, so small, should mate with the large raven, something also reported by no naturalist; but the following Midrash passage deserves attention for its completeness and closer specification. Mid. R. Bereschit fol. 72, col. 2 states: In the time of R. Chija Rabbah a starling came to Eretz Yisrael; the bird was brought before him and he was asked about its cleanness or uncleanness. The Rabbi answered: Let the bird be set on a roof, and let one see which bird, whether a clean or an unclean one, associates with it, since in that case it belongs to its kind. When this was done, the עורבא מיצראה “Egyptian raven” came and associated with the starling, in consequence of which it was declared unclean. This Egyptian, unknown species of raven will, being smaller than ours, perhaps be of the size of the starling; thus Aristotle (l. c. 8, 27, 4) expressly reports that the Egyptian ravens are smaller than ours; for עורבא מיצראה [p. 177] there also stands קורא מיצראה; see the appendix to this work.

The Midrash (ibid. fol. 84, col. c.) also has a proverb about the starling: אין שני זרזירים ישינים על דף אחד “Two starlings do not sleep on one board”, i.e. they are snappish and quarrelsome with one another. Perhaps in Midr. R. Wajikra fol. 202, col. b one should likewise think of the starling, where it is said there that the עורב hears words and betrays them. As is well known, the starling imitates much and pronounces much. On the head-nodding of the starling see §. 234.

Chulin 62b names eight birds in which the membranes of the stomach can indeed be peeled from one another, but only by means of a knife. The membranes are so firmly attached to one another that the stomach, even if it has lain in the sunshine for a considerable time, can still only be peeled with the knife. Now since the double membrane belongs to the distinguishing marks of a clean bird (§. 23), on account of this circumstance the doubt arose regarding the eight birds whether they are permitted to be eaten. Only in the case of one of them (§. 219) was the doubt converted into a definite ruling.

On the etymological discussion of the names of these eight birds the lexicographers maintain a stubborn silence, and if I have therefore attempted to offer etymological conjectures, I may well find an excuse in that relentless silence.
The Crested Lark.

The first of those eight birds is the חובא, in which I suspect the crested lark (Alauda cristata). In Aristotle (Thierg. 8, 18, 2) it is called Κόρυδος [korydos]; it hides itself in winter, lives singly and does not, like the skylark, migrate in large flocks to distant lands, whereas חוגא in the following article designates the latter species of lark. חובא, from חבא “to hide”, may indicate either the hiding of the lark in winter or the hiding of the nest under clods of earth. For the crested lark makes its nest under clods, thatched roofs and among garden plants, while the skylark often makes its nest merely in the hoofprints of cattle. That larks may be considered clean is probable because [p. 178] they belong to the sparrow family; cf. the following article.
The Lark.

The second of those eight birds is the חוגא (Chulin 62b). In Aram. חוגא has the meaning of turning around in a circle, which, as is well known, is the case with the lark. It rises spirally straight into the air, appearing at height like a ball turning about itself (see Voigt l. c. 2. p. 215), and so חוגא may perhaps mean the lark; however, I must note that the responsa חינוך בית יהודא on Jore Dea No. 32 expressly say: עוף שקורין לערכין בל"א שמעתי דהוא עוף טמא וכן אסרו אב"ד דק"ק פ"פ “The bird which in German is called Lerche is, as I have heard, an unclean bird, and it was also declared forbidden by the rabbi of Frankfurt.” But did these decisors also consider that the lark belongs to the (clean) sparrow family?
The Wren.

The third of those eight birds is the סוגא (Chulin 62b). The word סייג means fence, and from it סוגה enclosure; it is possible, then, that סוגא is the wren [German Zaunkönig, "fence-king"]. The bird is so called because it flutters singing from fence to fence (Beumer: Populäre Naturg. [=Aristotle, History of Animals (Historia animalium; German title Naturgeschichte)] p. 236).
The Brambling.

The fourth of those eight birds is the הרנתא (Chulin 62b). The word may be compounded of הר "mountain" and נתא (in the sense of נתה, to dwell). However, we must admit that the notion of dwelling on, or among, mountains is very elastic, and would be equally applicable to the mountain falcon, the mountain pheasant, the mountain magpie, the mountain thrush, etc.; but the brambling [German Bergfink, "mountain finch"] belongs to the sparrow genus, from which, as we have seen, some species have already been named (§. 213 and 214).
The Black Woodpecker.

The fifth of those eight birds is the כוחילנא (Chulin 62b), which Landau derives from כחל "black colour" and translates as black woodpecker. But who would wish to determine this explanation, here too, as the only correct one? There is a blackbird, a black tit, a black duck, etc., and so נקבל היא קבלה אם
—; it is only a pity that Landau gives his explanation a priori and merely at random.
The Coot.
The sixth of those eight birds is the בר נפחא (Chulin 62b) "son of blowing", perhaps the coot [German Blashuhn, "blowing hen"] (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 381). Landau wavers between coot and plover.
On בר see above p. 2, note *.
The Moorhen.

The seventh of those eight birds is the מרדא (Chulin 62b), which is also called תרנגולא דאגמא "cock of the reeds". Our passage states: At first there was doubt about the מרדא with regard to its purity; later Rabbi Papa said that the bird תרנגולא דאגמא is forbidden, whereas the bird תרנגולתא דאגמא "hen of the reeds" is permitted to be eaten; still later it was seen that the latter bird, too, presses its food firmly to the ground and tears pieces from it in the manner of birds of prey (§. 23), whereupon the eating of the תרנגולתא דאגמא, which is identical with the name גירוחא, was also forbidden.

The Tosephot (ibid.) rightly remark that no distinction is made here between cock and hen of one and the same species, since it is inconceivable that at first the male of the moorhen was forbidden and the female permitted; rather, two distinct species are meant here, of which the one was called תרנגולא דאגמא "reed cock" and the other תרנגולתא דאגמא "reed hen".
Most probably the different species of the moorhen are meant here; for there is a larger species and several smaller species (Voigt l. c.
[p. 180] 2. p. 380), of which the larger was presumably called תרנגולא "cock" and the smaller תרנגולתא "hen";

but perhaps the following distinction may have been made here: the תרנגולא דאגמא, which was also called מרדא "refractory", "wild", may be the wild bittern, which is untameable and fights even against the strongest dogs and is stubborn; it was regarded from the outset as forbidden, because it (Ardea stellaris) belongs to the heron genus (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 362); it is much larger than the moorhen and was therefore called תרנגולא "cock"; the moorhen, on the other hand, the smaller and easily tamed bird, was perhaps called גירותא for that reason, from גור "to dwell", "to abide", with reference to its capacity for staying in human habitation.

Difficult to determine is the following statement made by the Talmud. As an equivalent for the forbidden bird גירותא, the tongue of the כוורא (fish) is permitted to be eaten (Chulin 109b). Which fish is meant here is not said; the Tosephot (M. Katan 11a) also believe that a particular fish is to be assumed, but do not specify it further. I therefore venture to express a conjecture, although it admittedly does not agree with the view of Rashi. He takes גירותא in the latter Talmud passage and the same bird name at Chulin 62b as the name of one and the same bird, namely that of the moorhen, and the taste of this bird is said to be like the taste of the fish tongue. But why should the tongue of the fish in particular have a taste distinct from the rest of the fish's flesh? And which fish could this be? I, however, take the גירותא mentioned in Chulin 109b to be the name of the woodpecker. This bird has a horny tongue set with pointed, backward-directed spiny bristles, just like the tongue of the fish. I therefore derive גירותא from גרר, whence מגרה "saw", since the tongue of the woodpecker is set with spines like a saw. I need hardly say that this conjecture is highly daring, and I only remark further that Jalkut Schimoni (Ps. [=Psalms] fol. 130, col. 3), which enumerates several similar equivalents, leaves precisely גירותא and כוורא unmentioned; the same is the case in Midr. R. Wajikra fol. 191, col. 1.
The Steppe Lark.

The last of those eight birds, finally, is the הושלמי (Chulin 62b), of which it is said that it is very lustful and mounts many foreign birds (Sanhedrin 108a). Read also הלשמי, and this spelling might serve for the following identification. הל means "heap of rubble", and שמי "wasteland, steppe", and I would conjecture the steppe lark here. The reason for the doubt concerning the purity of the said eight birds was discussed above (§. 212). In these birds the membranes of the stomach are difficult to separate from one another, and in fact the lark has a muscular stomach, so that it can digest small stones in the manner of fowl (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 215). The muscular part is, as is well known, the inner hard membrane of the stomach, and in the lark it may be difficult to detach from the outer membrane.
More decisive is that statement about lustfulness, for the lark belongs to the sparrow genus, whose lustful nature is well known.

We now come again to a group of birds about which the commentaries and lexicographers give not the slightest information, and for which we are therefore once more reduced to attempting conjectures. Perhaps we shall succeed in at least offering a few guiding hints.
The Bullfinch.

Chulin 141b mentions a clean bird חימה. Also reads: חמאה. Here we have only to seek out the basic meaning of the root of that word. חימה means, first, wonderful, perfect, and one might think of the wonderful bird of paradise, which Scaliger (see Göthe and Zelter, Briefwechsel vol. 6, p. 96) calls Monstrum sine vitio; but this splendid bird belongs to the raven family and cannot count as a clean bird.
Secondly, חמאה means garlic, and, as is well known, larks, because they eat field garlic, have its pleasant taste;
[p. 182] but this reason is far too weak for thinking, on that account, of the lark in our passage (which in any case has a different name, see §. 214).

Thirdly, תם means simple, and so the stupid, guileless and incautious bullfinch may be meant here. Its simplicity has become proverbial; it belongs to the sparrow family and can therefore rightly have been regarded as a clean bird.

In the Midrasch Rabba (Schir ha-Schirim) the word תמתי, used of the dove, is rendered once (fol. 12, col. d) as beautiful and the second time (ibid. fol. 17, col. d beginning) as perfect; but the dove cannot be meant in our Talmud passage, since the Talmud never calls this bird תמתי.
The Penguin.

Chulin 62b mentions two birds: the בוניא is permitted to be eaten, the פרוא is forbidden to be eaten. There must be an essential contrast here in the nature of the two birds, and I believe I find it in the fact that פרוא is a lean bird (see the following article), and בוניא a fat one. Here we speak of the latter. Aruch reads כניא, which means fat. The fatty mesentery of cattle is called כנחא, which Münster [=Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), Hebraist; probably his Dictionarium Chaldaicum (Basel 1527)] (in the Lex.) explains as Sumen pinguendo intestinorum; I would therefore understand by בוניא the penguin (Spheniscus demersus; Voigt l. c. 2, p. 422). As a goose it may rightly have been declared clean. But our reading too could speak for our explanation, for while פרוא is the Avis prava, the lean bird, בוניא is the Avis bona, the good, i.e., fat bird; thus the quail, because of its fatness, is called in Arabic سَمَانِي [samānī], Samana (Rosenmüller loc. cit. p. 346).
The Sea Gull.

Like בוניא (§. 222), פרוא (Chulin 62b) is also a water bird, and in the latter name I suspect the very lean sea gull. The Hebrew שחף (Lev. 11, 16) is explained by most commentaries and lexicographers as gull, from שחף "emaciated", "lean", and this is quite especially the sea gull (Larus marinus [p. 183] in L.). The Talmudic פרוא may be formed from the Latin prava, "bad"; cf. the Judeo-German parva, by which one understands something re-melted, which is probably corrupted from prava. Cf. §. 378.
The Storm Gull.

Chulin 102b an unclean bird is called קלניחא, which Raschi explains as עוף כחוש מאוד "very lean bird"; the Greek Κηλὸν [kēlon] also means lean, dry, and so קלניחא, like פרוא (§. 223), may be a gull, namely the smallest species, the storm gull. This gull has many feathers but very little flesh, and is rightly the bird whose limbs (אבר), as our passage says, are not the size of an olive (כזית).

On B. batra 20a Raschi says: the קלניחא is so lean that no one eats it. In this passage it is also said that one may put the קלניחא into a child's hands, because it does not scratch; as is well known, all gulls can easily be kept as cage birds (Voigt l. c. 2, p. 388). On children playing with birds kept in the house see Job. 40, 29.
The Skua.

B. batra 20a, where the storm gull (§. 224) is discussed, mentions a bird that is כעין קלניחא "like the קלניחא, i.e., which is lean like the storm gull but not so peaceable; one does not put it into a child's hands, because it scratches. The skua cannot be kept as a cage bird, for it is particularly wild and rapacious.
The Bird of Paradise.

Berachoth 6b it says: In the coastal cities (כרכי ים) there is a bird called כרום which casts many colors at sunrise. There is no doubt that כרום is formed from Χρῶμα [chrōma], color, just as the Midrasch Rabba (Bereschit fol. 9, col. 2) calls a bird endowed with 365 colors צבוע "colored one" [p. 184] *). In our Talmud passage a bird must be named whose metallic-colored plumage shimmers variously in the sunlight, and that will probably be our splendid bird. The Spaniards call it Pajaro del sol (or Passaros de sol), sun bird, and indeed one believes one sees a shining ball of fire when the bird of paradise floats along in the air. It lives in the farthest East Indies, especially on New Guinea and the other Papuan islands, and was therefore known to seafarers, to which our passage alludes.
The Pelican.

Chulin 63a names four birds whose names were evidently formed from their shape. The first is called לקני and is permitted to be eaten. Apart from the fact that the word may perhaps have arisen from Πελεκὰν [pelekan] by dropping the first syllable, לקן also means "jug", "vessel", which is in a certain sense what the pouch stretching beneath the beak serves as. In this pouch, or cellular tissue, the bird holds the food it has taken in, which it then lets the young fetch from its throat; it thus has a vessel in which it keeps the food.
Cf. Appendix s.v. את הים
The Booby.

Chulin 63a, alongside the לקני (§. 227), the בטני is also named as a clean bird. The name (בטן) points to a thick- or broad-bellied bird, perhaps the gannet. The gannet too belongs to the pelican genus and is called Pelicanus bassanus, from the island of Bass, on which it multiplies greatly; perhaps, therefore, בטני may also have some affinity with bassanus; in any case, the pairing of לקני and בטני entitles us to think of the two birds of the related genus.
A Species of Gannet.

Chulin 93b it is said: The בטני (gannet §. 228) is permitted to be eaten, whereas the bird בטנאי is permitted to be eaten in some places and forbidden in some other places. Since the bird is not here declared absolutely unclean, one need only think of the difference between a more or less rigorous observance, and while some held the בטנאי, as a variety of the בטני, perhaps the sooty-brown species (Sula fusca), to be clean, others declared it unclean, as is the case with the various species of moorhen (§. 219).
The Bustard.

Chulin 63b, alongside בטנאי (§. 229), שקנאי is also mentioned; like the former, this bird too is eaten by some and not by others. We have already seen earlier (§. 201) שקי as a designation for the feet of birds, cf. also §. 202 and in addition the relevant Talmud passage, and so we also derive שקנאי from שק “shank,” by which the entire foot is designated. The bustard has long and strong feet, and may therefore have received its name שקנאי.

Some eat it because it resembles the turkey and is in general counted by some among the gallinaceous birds; others, however, on account of its thick, strong feet, placed it rather in the kinship of the aquiline birds. Cf. the cited Talmud passage.
The Wine-Drinker.

שהיא חמרא (Chulin 62b), which is forbidden to be eaten. The name points to a bird that eats the fruit of the vine, perhaps the redwing (Turdus iliacus), which is so called because it steals and eats grapes in the vineyards; it should be noted, however, that the common thrush (§. 262) is a clean bird, which incidentally still allows another bird of the same genus to be declared unclean, cf. §§. 219 and 229.
Perhaps here [p. 186] the vine lark (Alauda cristata) is meant; the common lark (§. 213) belongs to the eight birds doubtful with respect to cleanness
The Lapwing.

Chulin 62b the bird מוגא חמרא (mixed wine) is forbidden to be eaten. Here one must doubtless think of a wine-coloured bird. In Aelian (Thierg. 4, 58) it is called Οἰνάς [Oinas]; it is smaller than the wood pigeon (Φάσσα [Phassa]) and larger than the common pigeon (Περιστερά [Peristera]), and is, as several explain it, the lapwing, French Vanneau. The bird may be so called because it is metallic dark green on the back, like the grape.
A Wine-Coloured Bird.

Chulin 62b it is said that the bird בת מוגא חמרא (daughter of the מוגא חמרא, see §. 232) is permitted to be eaten. In Aristotle (Naturg. 9, 36, 4) a bird is called Οἰνάνθη [Oinanthē], which some explain as a kind of wild pigeon, so called from the colour of the ripening grape. Indeed the stock dove (Columba oenas in L.) has a wine-red breast, and it is therefore rightly permitted to be eaten as a pigeon. Another species of wild pigeon is spoken of elsewhere (§. 255); yet it cannot be surprising that the various species of wild pigeon bore different names; the species mentioned here lives in holes in trees, the one to be mentioned later lives in clefts.
Two Species of Birds.

Chulin 62a it says: The bird מרדו זגיד ואכיל is permitted to be eaten, the bird סגיד ואכיל is forbidden to be eaten. Rashi reads מרה for מרדו, probably because מרדו is mentioned earlier (§. 219) as an unclean bird. Possibly one must here look for such birds as shake their head more or less; thus, as is well known, the starling runs with constant nodding of the head. The lexica [p. 187] do not even have the roots of those words, and perhaps a distinction must be made here between סגר “to bend down” and זגר “to raise.” But I do not venture to put forward any further conjectures.
The Linnet.

Chulin 62b the bird צרדא is declared a clean bird. Landau translates flax finch or linnet, since צרדא means flax. The linnet belongs to the sparrow genus and is therefore rightly permitted to be eaten.
The Snow Finch.

Chulin 62b the bird ברדא (Aruch reads: בר אדא) is declared an unclean bird. On this Landau remarks: “Perhaps it is the snow finch, which received this name not only from the white colour of the throat, the breast and the entire lower part, but also because it inhabits the cold lands. It is found in great numbers on the snowy mountains of the Caucasus and in Persia.”

But the snow finch belongs to the sparrow genus and should probably rather count as a clean bird, cf. §. 235. Why could one not think of the alpine chough, which belongs to the raven genus? I therefore leave the choice to further research.
The Sparrow.

Chulin 65a it says: The bird ציפרתי catches food in the air. Rashi says the ציפרתי is a clean bird; in general, according to the Talmud (ibid. 139b), צפור is in every case a clean species of bird. Although צפור is indeed a generic name, צפור is nevertheless probably, like the Latin Passer, in general the sparrow; in Hebrew as in Arabic the root word means to chirp, from which the sparrow has its name. The Latin word seems to be formed by transposition from צפר, while the German Sperling contains the Hebrew word in its first syllable.
The Hummingbird.

In Succa 5b the giant bird (§. 502), as the extreme of size, is set against the צפרתא, similar to the juxtaposition of the two extremes of the unicorn and lice nits (§. 174), and so ציפורתא, with the diminutive ending תא, may denote a very small little bird, perhaps the hummingbird. Perhaps it is also meant in the passage (Temura 34a) in which it is said that it was customary to embroider the figure of birds on purses or similar objects made of hair. In any case ציפורתא denotes all kinds of small birds, similar to some other names by which small birds are called; cf. the following article.

We mention here some other names by which small kinds of birds are generally called. The frequently occurring פרגיות is explained in various ways: by Raschi on B. mez. 24b as גוזלות, which does not necessarily mean young pigeons, but simply young ones, here young small birds (see §. 1). On Berachoth 39a Raschi translates it as פרדריש, Perdrix, partridge, but inaccurately, although partridges do indeed also belong to the delicacies prepared from the flesh of young birds. The biblical אשתעשע (Ps. 119, 16) is rendered by the Chaldean as אתפרג "to delight oneself". Perhaps one should think of a kind of fricassee, stewed meat, from Frigo.
The Aruch explains the word as: תרנגולים קטנים "young chickens" and, still more generally, as: צפרים קטנים "young birds".
In the Midrasch Rabba (Bereschit fol. 19, col. 4) young fowl are called פרגין, and Rabba (Echa fol. 59, col. 3): פריגין (cf. also Tos. Chulin 62b. s.v. כרוי).
Another general name for young fowl is פרפראות (Berachoth 42a). Cf. Buxdorf (Lex. p. 1846), and צלצלא, cf. §. 252.
The Ostrich.
נעמית (Kelim 17, 14), נעמיתא (Sabbat 110b), בת נעמיתא (M. Katan 26a), בת יענה and בת יענה (Chulin 64b), pl. נעמיות (Rabba [p. 189] Bamidbar fol. 247, c).

In the first passage a vessel is mentioned that is made from a glazed ostrich egg. Such an egg has the contents of 24 hens' eggs and is therefore of considerable size (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 342). The contents of the egg were used in medicine (Sabbat 110b). The belief that the ostrich lives on indigestible things such as glass, iron and the like was erroneous; thus the Talmud calls broken glass the food of the ostrich (ibid. 128a); what is correct in it, however, is that the ostrich, owing to its poor sense of taste, swallows such objects, yet it lives on vegetable matter, which it consumes without discrimination; for which reason the statement of the Midrasch (Jalk. Schim. [=Yalkut Shimoni] part 2, fol. 17a) that the ostriches devoured the flesh of the slain Agag is incorrect.

In the passage Chulin 64b it is said of the ostrich that it stays with its young and mourns their loss. However, it is known that the ostrich in the tropical zone merely presses a hollow into the sand and leaves the hatching of the eggs to the sun. It lays near the nest a separate egg, which it tramples, so that the contents putrefy and produce maggots, on which the hatched ostriches live at first; nevertheless it is correct that on either side of the tropics it broods itself and defends nest and young with much courage.

The well-known stupidity of our bird may perhaps underlie the statement of Nachmanides (on Job 30, 29) that the ostrich remains silent even when it is beaten. Regarding the voracity of the bird mentioned above, let it be added that it once snatched away a Rabbi's prayer straps, whereupon he strangled it (Jerusalem Talmud M. Katan fol. 83b), and that pieces of gold bars the size of olives were thrown to it, which it swallowed and then passed out polished (Rabba Bamidbar fol. 247, c), in which connection one should think of the grinding down of the metal by the muscular stomach of the bird. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Joma ch. 4, Hal. 4) it is stated in more detail: the pieces of gold were coated with dough and thrown to the ostriches, which swallowed them and thereby cleansed them (מסננין).
The Peacock.

טוס (B. Kama 55a) טוס (Sabbat 130a), and in the parallel passage (Chulin 116a): טוסא. Gr. Ταώς [Taōs], just as Raschi [p. 190] on the first and last passages translates the word as פוואן, Paon; the female: טוסמ (Jerusalem Talmud B. Kama 5a). In the first passage it is said that one may not crossbreed the domestic hen and the peacock, although they are raised together.

In the two other passages it is related that someone served his guest the head of a peacock cooked in milk (or perhaps with milk set out at the same time), which he also ate, because in that place it was permitted to eat fowl cooked with milk.

That the head and not another part of the body was prepared as a tasty dish may have its reason in that the head is perhaps the tastiest part of the peacock, for its flesh is anything but that; it is rather hard and lean, and the bird is kept only for ornament (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 306). From our passage it follows at the same time that the peacock is a clean bird; nevertheless it is not now declared clean; cf. Landau (Aruch s.v. נגר). Cf. p. 184,
The Goose.
אוז (B. mez. 91b), אווזא (Joma 84a*), pl. אוזין (Sebachim 70b), קוקא (from quacking, §. 108, pl. קאקי, Gittin 73a).

Levita (in the Tishbi) says: “From אוז the pl. is אוזים, from אווזא the pl. is אווזות, more correctly אווזאות,” which, however, Buxdorf (Lex. p. 39) rightly disputes, since both the emphatic א and the א of the feminine ending are lost in the pl. The domestic goose differs from the wild one (§. 243) in that it has a longer bill (קועיה Rashi: ביק, Bec**), and in that the male has the penis and the testicles further below the diaphragm, whereas in the male of the wild goose they lie higher up. With this compare Aristotle (Thierg. 3, 1, 4); he says, in other words, that in the goose, soon after copulation, the testes, which lie below the diaphragm, [p. 191] become visible; apart from this time the testes (in the form of two acorns) lie further down; now, since the wild goose is smaller and slimmer, the testes will probably be visible on top at all times, which is what is meant in our Talmud passage.

The two species further differ in that the domestic goose has several eggs on the ovary at the same time, whereas the wild goose gets an egg on the ovary only once it has laid the previous one (B. Kama 55a). For these reasons of difference the two species may not be crossed with each other.
It should be noted that Sch. Aruch [=Shulchan Aruch] (Yoreh De'ah §. 297, 7) gives only that second, admittedly most essential, distinguishing criterion. —

The goose is a water bird and therefore, after the manner of these birds, has a very thin cerebral membrane (Chulin 56b). If one holds the goose's wings up, it still walks on, whereas the hen then draws its feet up as well and thus cannot walk. (Sabbat 128b; this lies in the difference of the muscular system of the two birds.) The flat side of the goose's foot is as broad as it is long (Bechoroth 45a). As a rule the goose returns to the coop in the evening (Beza 24a), yet it sometimes leaves the house and settles in gardens (Chulin 38b). The cackling of geese gave rise to the saying: He who sees a goose in a dream may hope for wisdom, for thus it is written (Spr. Sal. [=Proverbs (German Sprüche Salomo's)] 1, 20): Wisdom cries aloud outside (Berachoth 57a); the goose also sometimes emits a whistling sound, which it produces through the nostrils with the bill closed; Rashi (Aboth 2, 10) calls this sound: שיפלור, siffler. Geese (the Jerusalem Talmud Ketuboth 26, d adds hens as well) cry out when someone suddenly passes by them (Ketuboth 27a); in another passage there (B. batra C. 8. H. 7) the expression is found: כדון אכון קקו פריפט “You cackle like geese.”

The exclamation “White geese!” expressed a rebuke against judges who were hoary and yet self-seeking; people said: “The white geese strip people of their cloaks” (Gittin 73a). With the same expression a rabbi paid women a not very delicate compliment: “He can,” he said, “remain unmoved at the sight of women, for they seem to him like white geese” (Berachoth 20a); from this passage we take merely the element of dazzling whiteness, such as the feathers of some geese possess.

[p. 192] The uses of this bird are manifold. Besides the eating of its flesh, the fat in the uppermost little wing joint (כנייל, probably כניכל, knuckle) also served against mouth rot (Joma 84a*). For external diseases of the mouth the mixture was applied with a bird's feather (Gittin 86a). The lung had special medicinal power. People used to say: “A goose costs one Sus, but the lung alone costs four Susin” (Chulin 49a); here, to be sure, the medicinally prepared goose lung is meant. The down feather (פלומא, Pluma, which, however, is more correctly called מלט, Molasse §. 76) was laid on the spot of the lung of a slaughtered animal that was thought to be injured, for the slightest draught of air passing through the injured membrane when the lung is inflated sets the feather in motion (ibid. 46b). Finally, geese were used for threshing (Sanhedrin 29b).
On the moulting of the goose cf. §. 246, note ***.
The Wild Goose.

אזז בר (B. Kama 55a). One may not cross it with the domestic goose, since the two species differ in many respects. The female of the wild goose always has only one egg on the ovary, whereas the domestic one has many eggs on the ovary at the same time; in the male of the wild goose the testes lie higher up, in that of the domestic goose lower down, but in both below the diaphragm (see §. 242); finally, the wild goose has a shorter bill than the domestic one. Although קועיה means neck both in quadrupeds (B. Kama ibid.) and in birds (Chulin 28a), Rashi nevertheless translates the word in our Talmud passage by ביק, Bec, bill, because in fact the bill of the wild goose is much shorter than that of the domestic goose, whereas the neck in both species is equally large in proportion to size. Cf. the appendix s.v. אזז הים.
The Duck.

בר אוזא (Beza 32b). The prefixed בר, בן, or בת does indeed designate the young of the animal (§. 1), yet בר אוזא does not mean “young goose” but, as it were, “little goose,” just as Latin Anas is related to Anser; cf. on this my contribution in the “Lien d’Israél” (2nd year, p. 364). In Jehuda ha-Lewi (in the Kusari ch. 3, §. 35) the duck is called אלברכיה, Arabic اَلْبَرْكِيَةُ [al-barkiyatu].

The duck has the habit of running to and fro with lowered head, rooting everywhere with its bill to seek food, and at the same time constantly looking about. From this arose the proverb: שפיל ואזיל בר אוזא ועיניה מטייפי “The duck stoops and walks on, and its eyes roam about,” by which a twofold thing was designated: first, a gossiping woman who sits at the distaff and meanwhile occasionally chatters and gossips about others (Megilla 14b), just as the duck searches while looking about, at the same time going forward.
Secondly, that proverb denoted the necessity of man, who, however weak he may be, must nevertheless look about for spiritual and physical nourishment (B. Kama 92b).

The two skins of the stomach are sometimes so firmly attached to each other that they can be peeled apart only after the stomach has been exposed to the warmth of the sun for a fairly long time (Chulin 62b).
They were accustomed either to roast them (Beza 32b), or to prepare them as a pastry (פשטידא, Pâté, cf. my contribution in Frankel’s Monatsschrift 1856. p. 441) (Pesachim 74b).

Stomach and entrails were sometimes prepared into a dish with a thin dough (Tos. ibid. s.v. טפל); otherwise the entrails were little esteemed, and were thrown to the cat (Sabbat 142b). In the parallel passage to this (Beza 32b) Raschi has את for בר אוזא, which is probably a misprint.
The Harlequin Duck.
In Chulin 57a it is said: Someone brought a basket of אינקורי; Raba then examined the place where the thigh sinews converge (צומת הגידין, §. 73), and thereupon permitted the birds to be eaten.

Here Raschi gives two explanations of the word אינקורי; [p. 194] according to the one, they were slaughtered birds whose feet had been chopped off up to above the thighs, so that the Rabbi could establish the cleanness of the birds only from the thighs. According to this, אינקורי would be the same as נקורי (as Aruch also reads), from נקר: stabbed off, broken off; the other explanation, on the other hand, reads: ובתשובת הגאונים מצאתי עוף שחור הוא ושל מים הוא ובמצחו חברבורות לבנות ועל שם כך נקרא אינקורי שהוא מנומר כמו ניקוב פינטורה “In the Responsa of the Geonim I found that it is a black water bird; on its forehead it has white spots, and it is therefore called אינקורי, since it is spotted, so to speak, perforated, in the sense of Pointure.”
The white spot on the forehead, namely, forms the reflection of the white colour on a black ground, and from a distance looks like a black perforated object.

According to this description we would have to think of the harlequin duck (Anas histrionica); it is black with a lead-grey breast and has a white spot in the region of the eyes. Voigt l. c. 2. p. 399.
The Chicken.
Masc. תרנגול and תרנגולא (Beza 25b), pl. תרנגולין (B. Kama 17a), further שכוי (R. ha-Schana [=Rosh Hashanah] 26a), נרגול (Sanhedrin 63b) and גבר (Joma 20b).

The hen is called תרנגולת (Beza 2a), גברית (Sabbat 67b*) and is called סכות by some (Sanhedrin 63b). Incorrect is the explanation of Raschi's teacher (Gittin 69b) that חמימתא means the hen, cf. §. 255.

The brooding hen is called וגזא (Bechoroth 8b). It is further called, on account of its cackling: פחיא (the same as from פעיא, from פעה, Beza 7a). Fattened chickens: ברבורים אבוסים (B. mez. 86b**). The chick is called: רצוצא (§. 1).

[p. 195] There are white, black and red chickens (A. Sara [=Avodah Zarah] 14b). The feathers are lost through moulting***). Once a hen lost its feathers completely; then it was wrapped in a leather apron, then placed on a warm spot of the oven, whereupon new feathers came forth, and this new growth even surpassed the former feathers in fullness (Chulin 57b).

The chicken whets its beak (§. 48) on the ground in order to dry it after it has drunk (Teharoth 3, 8). On its head it has a comb (קרישתא, Crête, Sanhedrin 105b). This usually has red spots*), which, however, are invisible in the first three hours of the day, since the comb is entirely pale at this time (Berachoth 7a). The cock is also mostly accustomed to stand on one foot at this time (ibid.). If one cuts off the cock's comb, it becomes sad and no longer treads (Sabbat 110b). When sleeping, the chicken keeps itself up high, usually on a beam or some other object raised in the air, which place it seeks out for its night's rest at the onset of dusk (Sabbat 35b). But since this place is sometimes in a chimney, or elsewhere where the smoke rises, this could be harmful to the chicken's eye; therefore nature has arranged that in the chicken, during considers it a large bird originating from the Beberéi; here, however, we have only to take the Talmudic view into account.

[p. 196] sleep, the lower eyelid covers the upper, and the smoke thus passes over the eye (Sabbat 77b†). When flying it creates a strong current of air, so that once, as a result, a vessel fell to the ground and broke (B. Kama 17a). If one lifts the chicken up by the wings, it cannot walk on its feet, since it draws them up of its own accord (Sabbat 128b; for the reason for this see §. 242).

The crowing of the cock shattered a glass vessel into which it had stuck its head (Kiduschin 24b; based on laws of acoustics). The cock crows at daybreak (Berachoth 60b); people therefore avoided leaving the dwelling before cockcrow, i.e., before the break of day, since the night-time can more easily bring about various accidents (Joma 21a*). Superstition fears crowing**) late at night, as well as the occasionally heard crowing of a hen (Sabbat 67b).
The chicken and the bat are contrasted as opposites of the Animalia nocturna and diuturna. The cock says to the latter: I may hope for the daylight, for the day belongs to me! (Sanhedrin 68b***).

The hen sometimes lays its egg on dung heaps, but never on a sloping spot where it could easily roll down and be broken (Sabbat 42b). At first the egg hangs on the stalk, but detaches itself once it has acquired its shell (Temura 31a). The egg requires 10 days for its formation and 21 days of brooding (Bechoroth 8a; on Rashi's erroneous explanation of this passage cf. §. 17). The egg that is taken out of a slaughtered hen after its death, as well as the egg that the hen conceives by lying in sun-warmed sand, [p. 197] are not capable of being hatched (§. 183). According to Aristotle (Thierg. 6, 2, 6), however, wind-eggs can still be made fertile if the hen, during the time in which the yolk has not yet been changed into the white, is still fertilized by a bird of the other sex*).

The eggs resulting from being trodden by the cock the hen lays only by day, whereas the wind-eggs also at night (Beza 7a). Treading takes place among fowl only by day (ibid.). The hen refrains from lying down in warm sand if a cock is near her, or at least so near that she can hear his crowing by day (when the echo of sound does not carry as far as at night) (ibid.). The hen then seeks out the cock, and if there is a river between her and the cock, she crosses the bridge, which she refrains from doing only if the crossing is attended with danger (ibid.). The hen sometimes abandons eggs on which she has already begun to brood, and one must then bring her back if the eggs are not to spoil; one can, however, also let another hen continue brooding the eggs (Pesachim 55b). In general, the fowl sometimes leave their dwelling and settle in gardens (Chulin 138b). A proper nest, however, the heavy birds do not, as is well known, build for themselves. The time of egg-laying is not always the same; as a rule the hen lays every other day (see in detail (Nidda 39b).

Fowl are very lustful, and the cock never goes far from the hens (Berachoth 22a). He courts the hens before he treads them (Erubin 100b). The extraordinary fertility of fowl (17 hens on a parsonage farm in the year 1821 laid no fewer than 3568 eggs, thus on average 209 eggs per hen; Voigt l. c. 2. p. 43) gave rise to the custom of carrying a pair of fowl before a bridal couple on their wedding day (Gittin 57a). Hen's eggs are cooked through the most quickly (Sabbat 80b, which admittedly refers to the eggs of large birds, such as ducks, geese etc.). The cock is, among [p. 198] the birds, the most wanton and is very hardy (iy, Rashi: אנדריש, endurci, Beza 25b); he is quarrelsome and inclined to bite against other cocks (Pesachim 113b), and particularly notorious in this respect were the cocks from the house of Bakia; they tolerated no intruders in their midst (Jebamoth 84a). Once a cock killed a child by pecking at its skull with its beak (Berachoth 27a).

Hen droppings (whose smell varies, see p. 55, note*) are dangerous for cattle and animals if they eat them (Chulin 58b); yet they are used for medicinal purposes (Gittin 69b, but erroneously, since a different bird is meant there, see §. 255).

Another use of the hen in medicine was that one who is bitten by a snake on a limb puts that limb into a hen torn apart alive, whereby the poison is drawn out (Joma 83b). Peculiar was the use of fowl for threshing (B. mez. 91b).

The best among poultry is a hen that stays among wine presses and, through feeding on grape skins, sometimes becomes so fat that it cannot step over a reed lying in its way (B. mez. 86b). Fowl like to eat vetch (Terumoth 11, 9); they also scratch on dung heaps and consume insects and worms, which they swallow alive (Kelim, 8, 5); for this reason fowl were not kept in Jerusalem, because they might scratch up defiling objects (B. Kama 82b). Although the hen, while scratching on dung heaps, remains unmolested by the weasels living there (Pesachim 8b), one nevertheless had to make the air holes in the hen coops so small that weasels could not get in through them (Sabbat 146a and b).

White fowl were preferably chosen for pagan sacrifices (A. Sara 13b; cf. on this Or. Chajim [=Orach Chayyim (part of the Shulchan Aruch)] §. 605), and the cock served superstition as an omen at the conclusion of a business transaction (Horajoth 12a). Finally it may be mentioned that the blood of the hen has different colors; that which streams out of the neck veins is red, that in the limbs is darker, i.e. blackish-red, and that in the entrails is saffron-yellow (§. 80). The following Midrash passage (Rabba Wajikra fol. 193, d) may also find its place here; it reads: “As long as the chicks are young, the mother hides them under her wings, warms them and gathers food for them; but as soon as they have grown up and one of them still wants to cling to its mother, [p. 199] she pecks it on the head and says to it: ““Scratch on your own dung heap!""
The Dove.
Given the numerous species of the dove genus
more than a hundred of them are counted

it is necessary from the outset to name the species mentioned in the Talmud, though some species cannot be determined with apodictic certainty. In all there are ten species, namely a) the domestic pigeon, of which three varieties occur, b) the turtledove in three varieties, c) the veiled pigeon, d) the tumbler pigeon, and e) the wild pigeon in two varieties.
Generic names for dove are: יונה (Berachoth 53b); the young dove: בן יונה (Chulin 22a, usually occurring in the pl. בני יונים) and בר גוזלא (ibid. 76b).
גוזל (see §. 1, note ***) denotes both the young and the year-old dove (cf. גוזל בן שנה, Gittin 56b), and with this name Rashi explains the פרידה occurring in B. mez. 84b, cf. §. 239.
The young that is not yet fledged is called: ניפול (Pullus, B. batra 23a).
The House Dove.

Of this species of dove there are three varieties: a) יונה עליה, i.e., the dove that lives in the upper rooms of the house; b) יונה שובך, doves that are kept in dovecotes, and c) יונה הרדיסאות, doves which, like the first two kinds, live either in the house or in the dovecote, but differ from them in that they remain constantly in their dwelling and do not seek their food outside.

This distinction is drawn still more precisely as follows: the יונה עליה stays throughout the day in the field or elsewhere outside, and returns in the evening to the house, where a nest has been prepared for it in the upper rooms.

The יונה שובך likewise stays outside during the day, but returns at evening to the dovecote; both kinds were also accustomed to nest in holes in the rocks, or in jars that had been set into the city walls expressly for this purpose.

From both kinds the יונה הרדיסאות differs, which does not go away from the dovecote or from the house (Beza 24a). The latter name is explained either as a proper place name and accordingly also [p. 200] read הדרסיאות (in which case one should perhaps think of the southern part of the Lebanon range, inhabited by Druze, cf. Schwarz: תוצאות הארץ pag. 6), or as a personal name after King Herod (Chulin 139b). He is said, as Maimuni (Chulin 12, 1) says, to have been the first to attempt to domesticate doves*).

This last dove is thus the house dove (Columba domestica) in the most proper sense, and further differs from the first two kinds in that, owing to its training, it is more easily caught, whereas those flutter about in the dovecote or in the nest and are less easily seized (Beza 24a).

(Continuation). In some passages doves and ravens are set up as opposites. In Meharaba there were two families, one was called: בי יונה (House of the Dove), the other: בי עורבתי (House of the Raven); the former enjoyed respect, the other fell into contempt (Kiduschin 70b). Further it is related: There was a man who was versed in the language of birds; he fell into captivity and one day heard the call of a raven: “Ilisch, Ilisch, flee, flee!” But Ilisch, for so that man was named, said: “I do not believe the lying bird.”

Then a dove came and likewise called those words to him, whereupon Ilisch said: “This bird I believe, for Israel is compared to the dove” (Gittin 45a). The faculty of speech of animals is treated in §. 39; here we take from the two Talmud passages only the point that the raven is cunning and thievish, whereas the dove is gentle and mild, and it is the Midrash especially that richly exploits the comparison of Israel with the dove; of the many passages we refer only to Midr. Rabba [=Midrash Rabbah] Schir ha-Schirim fol. 12, col. 4.

The dove is persecuted more than any other by other birds, while it itself does harm to none; but precisely for this reason it, an image of quiet gentleness, is deemed worthy among all birds to be chosen for sacrifice (B. Kama 93a), and, [p. 201] since it lives in the strictest monogamy, it serves as a symbol of chastity (Erubin 100b). That comparison of Israel with the dove is frequently expressed in the Talmud and is variously presented by the commentaries. Rashi (on Sabbat 130a) says: The dove does not defend itself with its beak like other birds, but with its wings, and further (on Berachoth 53b): The dove either flies away or defends itself with its wings, and what the wings are to the dove, the Law is to Israel, by which it preserves and maintains itself in all persecutions.

The Tosephot (Sabbat 49a, s.v. כנפיה), on the other hand, explain that every other bird, when it is tired, settles down to rest, whereas the dove lets one wing rest while it flies on with the other; thus Israel seeks strength in its persecution. As regards this latter point of natural history, it is well known that doves sometimes fly up and down for several hours, and the bird of prey in their vicinity flies off without booty after vain exertion; the muscular strength of the dove must therefore indeed be great.

From the Midrash passage mentioned above we take only the point that the dove does not leave the dovecote even when its young are taken from it. This assertion is not shared by Buffon. He regards the doves of our dovecotes as always only half-domesticated animals, for they like to live in larger company, and thus sometimes leave their abode.
We note only further that that Midrash passage also mentions the decoy dove; it says there: In the dovecote a dove was fed which by its scent*) lured other doves to it.

(Conclusion). As long as the doves cannot yet fly, they move at most 50 cubits away from the dovecote, or in general [p. 202] only so far as not to lose sight of the dovecote (Beza 11a). With regard to age, various points in time were designated according to which certain ritual rulings were made. As long as the dove is still so young that no blood flows when the feathers are plucked, it is unfit for sacrifice and does not yet belong to the category of בני יונה which the Law (Lev. 1, 14) designates for sacrifice. On the other hand, it bears the latter name as long as it has not yet acquired the metallic-coloured (צהב) feathers around the neck; but as soon as these feathers appear it ceases to be called בני יונה, yet receives the name תור (which denotes not so much the turtle-dove in particular as the full-grown dove in general) only once the remaining feathers have become yellow-coloured (זהב) (Chulin 22b). This designated interval thus forms a provisional state in which the dove is called neither בני יונה nor תור. In young doves, skin and flesh are equally soft (ibid. 76b).

It was believed that the dove has no gall (Jore Dea §. 42, 8), which Isidorus (Orig. lib. 12) and Sedulius (L. 2, Carm.) also report; it does, however, have a gall, which is located in the mesentery (Plin. h. n. [=Pliny the Elder, Natural History (Naturalis historia)] 11, 37, 75).

When drinking, the dove sucks up the water without raising its head (Chulin 62b), and the water does not flow back out of the beak (Para 9, 3), whereas the latter is the case with the tumbler pigeon (§. 254).
The common house pigeon and the tumbler pigeon sometimes hatch each other's eggs (Chulin 140b).

A particularly destructive enemy of doves is the marten, which is why the ladder was kept four cubits away from the dovecote, so that the predator could not jump into it (B. batra 22b). The fertility of doves is great, for except in the month of Adar (a late winter month) they breed every month and bring forth a pair, male and female. After two months the young doves already lay eggs and brood (B. batra 80a). King Janai had a mountain on which stood a tree from which 40 measures of young doves (קובייש, couvées) were taken down three times a month (Berachoth 44a); but here it is more probably the wild dove (§. 255) that is meant.
The flesh of young doves is tasty, and a notorious glutton named Ben Narboni consumed for dessert (!)
[p. 203] the trifle of 4 measures of young doves (Keritot 28a.*).

For all this, the dove also causes much damage.
